We is settled, and the margin table gives a clearer picture. On the 81 natural-Here problems that E5 flips, We and Let tie (21.0 vs 19.8, 9 gained and 8 lost). Where natural Let is confident (margin above 1), We costs about 8 points (34.7 to 26.7). On the problems E5 leaves in Here (margin below about -2), We is no better either. So We adds nothing to what E5 already does, and I'm closing it as a candidate. E5's policy of keeping confident problems and moving the weak "Here's" register looks right.

What I've gained is a usable tool: a prompt-end write that can pick the first token at will, at a cost of one generation pass per opener. Since the session runs until all passes are used, the budget isn't what's limiting me. What matters is choosing tests that can change the decision. Before planning the rest, I want to reread the early part of my notes, because the restarted view only shows the last 8,000 characters. I don't want to repeat a closed line, and I want to see what I learned about loops, since the Let register's higher cut-off rate is the most obvious cost of E5. This uses no pass, so it can't confirm or refute anything by itself. It's there to make sure the next hypotheses are actually new.

The notes confirm what's closed: loop rescue (twice), arithmetic and operand gain, retrieval gain, context steering, goal statements, operator bias, and variable binding. That leaves first-token register as the only causal lever with a real effect, and the only tested opener styles are Let, Here and now We. All three belong to chat or contest-style solutions. Nothing has tested the plain style the reference solutions use (for example "First find ..."), or structured formats such as "Step 1:".

I'll do this without guessing strengths. One teacher-forced pass on the original model gives exact first-token logprobs for ten hand-picked openers on 102 DEV prompts, because appending an opener to a prompt makes the tool report its logprob directly. Those numbers show which openers the prompt-end write can reach. Top-3 output also shows how each one continues, which previews the register. I'm dropping E7c now, so that the active edit and my notes agree.

If some openers sit within reach, roughly the same gap We had or less, I'll test them in generation on `dev_a1`, keeping the head-to-head on the same problems. If they're all far below We, I'd need a second write site or else close the line.

All ten openers are single tokens, E7c is dropped so no edits are active, and the plan is in the notes. I'll now run the screen on the original model. The result only sets priorities: an opener's logprob tells me how far it is from winning, and says nothing about how good its register would be. I'll use the gap to separate openers the existing write can reach from those it can't, and the continuation to tell which ones lead to a truly different style. Only generation can then show whether any of them beats Let.

Now the calibration table. For each opener I'll compute its mean first-token logprob and its gap to the best natural opener across the 102 prompts, and print how the top continuation token splits, using a fixed list of ordinary words only. As a reference for reachability, We needed a gap of about -9.5 at the strength that won on 94% of prompts, and that strength is near the saturation ceiling. An opener at a similar or smaller gap is reachable with the existing write. One with a gap beyond about -12 would need a second write site.
